title: The LORD Is Slow to Anger
subtitle: Nahum 1
description: Before the sentence, the character of God: avenging and slow to anger, a stronghold for those who trust Him.
paragraphs: The book is one page of address and three chapters of aim. This is the burden against Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite, and after that first line the prophet never appears again. Amos wept in his book and Micah went barefoot in his; Nahum is a voice and nothing else. The text gives him no hometown that anyone can find on a map, no king, no year. It dates itself only by what has happened and what has not: Thebes, in the third chapter, has already fallen, and Nineveh still stands. And Nineveh is a name this series has heard before. In Jonah's book the city repented and was spared. No call to repent is offered here. The book opens by telling you who God is, and it keeps the two halves of Him in one breath: “The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and full of wrath. The LORD takes vengeance on His foes and reserves wrath for His enemies.”

The very next line refuses to let wrath be the whole story, and it stands in the same poem, unseparated: “The LORD is slow to anger and great in power; the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. His path is in the whirlwind and storm, and clouds are the dust beneath His feet.” Slow to anger is not a slogan here. Between Jonah's mercy and this sentence on the same city lie generations of Nineveh's cruelty, and the delay is the slowness measured out in years. He is slow. He is not absent, and the guilty will not be left unpunished.

Then the poem shows what it looks like when He comes. “He rebukes the sea and dries it up; He makes all the rivers run dry. Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon wilts.” The richest pasture and orchard land in Israel's world, scorched by a rebuke. “The mountains quake before Him, and the hills melt away; the earth trembles at His presence”, and with the earth, “the world and all its dwellers.” And then the questions no one answers: “Who can withstand His indignation? Who can endure His burning anger? His wrath is poured out like fire; even rocks are shattered before Him.”

Out of that fire the book sets down its comfort, the verse Judah was meant to carry out of the chapter: “The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him.” The same God, the same chapter. A stronghold for those who trust, and for the city that spent centuries making prey: “But with an overwhelming flood He will make an end of Nineveh and pursue His enemies into darkness.” The plotting is answered before it is named: “Whatever you plot against the LORD, He will bring to an end. Affliction will not rise up a second time.” And the plotters themselves are pictured twice in one line, tangled and then burned: “For they will be entangled as with thorns and consumed like the drink of a drunkard”, and then, “like stubble that is fully dry.” The city is addressed to its face: “From you, O Nineveh, comes forth a plotter of evil against the LORD, a counselor of wickedness.” The text never names him. Neither does this retelling.

The last movement of the chapter turns fully to Judah, and it is release spoken in the first person. This is what the LORD says: “Though they are allied and numerous, yet they will be cut down and pass away. Though I have afflicted you, O Judah, I will afflict you no longer. For I will now break their yoke from your neck and tear away your shackles.” Assyria's alliance can be as numerous as it likes; the yoke has an end date now. For Nineveh the sentence is a grave. The LORD has issued a command concerning you, O Nineveh: “There will be no descendants to carry on your name. I will cut off the carved image and cast idol from the house of your gods; I will prepare your grave, for you are contemptible.” And Judah's chapter closes with a lookout posted. “Look to the mountains”, and what he sees is “the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace!” Isaiah saw those same feet on the same mountains in his own book, and said it in nearly the same words; each book tells it whole, in its own place. “Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows. For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off.” The feasts can be kept again. The marching is over.

title: The River Gates Are Open
subtitle: Nahum 2
description: The fall narrated as scene: red shields, the river gates open, the pool draining, the lions' den empty.
paragraphs: The second chapter does not argue. It watches. The fall of Nineveh is narrated as a scene unfolding in front of the reader, beginning with a warning shouted at a city that cannot use it: “One who scatters advances against you, O Nineveh.” Then the commands come in a volley, each one useless the moment it is spoken: “Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength!” Guard everything. It will not be enough, and the text knows it, because the very next verse leaves the battlefield entirely. In the middle of the siege narration stands a promise about somebody else: “For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob like the splendor of Israel, though destroyers have laid them waste and ruined the branches of their vine.” The seam is left standing exactly there, comfort planted inside the battle, because the battle is the comfort. Jacob's splendor is being restored by the same stroke that empties Nineveh.

Then the attacking army fills the frame, and the description is all color and speed. “The shields of his mighty men are red; the valiant warriors are dressed in scarlet. The fittings of the chariots flash like fire on the day they are prepared, and the spears of cypress have been brandished.” Scarlet and fire, and then motion that outruns its own horses: “The chariots dash through the streets; they rush around the plazas, appearing like torches, darting about like lightning.” They are already in the streets and plazas, inside the city that was told to guard the road.

Nineveh's own commanders get one verse, and in it they are falling over themselves: “He summons his nobles; they stumble as they advance. They race to its wall; the protective shield is set in place.” Too late, and the next verse is the shortest account of an empire ending in the whole book: “The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses.” The rivers were Nineveh's moat and pride, and the water does the breaching. What follows is decree, not battle: “It is decreed that the city be exiled and carried away; her maidservants moan like doves, and beat upon their breasts.” The city that exiled nations is exiled, in her own grammar.

The picture the chapter keeps is water running out. “Nineveh has been like a pool of water throughout her days, but now it is draining away.” Officers shout for the fleeing to stop, stop, and no one turns back. And over the draining pool comes the conqueror's order, the only words the invaders speak in the chapter: “Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!” “There is no end to the treasure, an abundance of every precious thing.” Centuries of other nations' wealth, stored in one place, now carried out the gates. The result is three hammer blows and a census of terror: “She is emptied! Yes, she is desolate and laid waste! Hearts melt, knees knock, bodies tremble, and every face grows pale!”

The chapter closes by walking through the empty royal menagerie. Nineveh's kings had pictured themselves as lions for centuries, and the prophet asks the den: “Where is the lions’ lair or the feeding ground of the young lions, where the lion and lioness prowled with their cubs, with nothing to frighten them away?” Nothing answers. The memory of the den is recited like an obituary: “The lion mauled enough for its cubs and strangled prey for the lioness. It filled its dens with the kill, and its lairs with mauled prey.” Mauled prey was the empire's economy, the world dragged home in pieces. And then God speaks the sentence the whole scene has been serving, in the first person, with the declaration set in the middle of it where the text sets it: “Behold, I am against you,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will reduce your chariots to cinders, and the sword will devour your young lions. I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voices of your messengers will no longer be heard.” The lion's prey is cut off from the earth. The den goes silent, and so does the chapter.

title: Woe to the City of Blood
subtitle: Nahum 3
description: The charges read out, the harlot exposed, and Thebes argued as the precedent Nineveh cannot escape.
paragraphs: The third chapter stops watching the fall and reads the charges. It opens with the woe, the funeral word the prophets pronounce over the living: “Woe to the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey.” City of blood is her title now. And before any charge is itemized, the assault is heard again, sound before sight: “The crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot!”

The carnage gets one verse and no more, in the text's own terms: “Charging horseman, flashing sword, shining spear; heaps of slain, mounds of corpses, dead bodies without end”, and the living, “they stumble over their dead”. The retelling leaves it there, one pass, the way the text leaves it, because the chapter is in a hurry to name the reason. The reason is a figure, and the figure is a woman who sold nations: “because of the many harlotries of the harlot, the seductive mistress of sorcery, who betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft.” Nineveh's empire had run on seduction as much as on swords, treaties and trade and sorcery drawing peoples in and betraying them. That is the charge the sentence answers.

The sentence is the refrain of the whole book, spoken a second time, with the declaration standing in the middle of it: “Behold, I am against you,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms. I will pelt you with filth and treat you with contempt; I will make a spectacle of you.” The seductress is exposed before the nations she seduced, and the exposure is the punishment's point: spectacle. What the onlookers say when they see her is quoted in their own voice: “Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?” No one steps forward. God's own question closes the verse, and it is almost gentle compared to what surrounds it: “Where can I find comforters for you?” There are none to find.

Then the book argues its precedent the way a lawyer argues a decided case. “Are you better than Thebes, stationed by the Nile with water around her, whose rampart was the sea, whose wall was the water?” Thebes, the great city of Egypt, defended by the Nile itself, a river for a rampart and water for a wall. And her strength was not only geography: “Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength; Put and Libya were her allies.” Boundless strength, named allies, a river for a wall. Nineveh has nothing Thebes did not have more of.

And Thebes fell, in the book's shortest obituary: “Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity. Her infants were dashed to pieces at the head of every street. They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains.” Exile, captivity, lots cast for her nobles like merchandise, and her infants killed in the streets, told in one line because the text tells it in one line. The episode ends where the argument ends. A greater city, behind a greater river, with greater allies, already lies in the past tense of this book. Nineveh is reading her own future in Thebes' file, and the file is closed.

title: No Healing for Your Injury
subtitle: Nahum 3
description: Figs for fortresses, locusts for an empire, sleeping shepherds, and a wound with no healing.
paragraphs: The verdict on Thebes becomes a verdict on Nineveh with two words: you too. “You too will become drunk; you will go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy.” The mistress of nations, hiding. And her defenses are priced like fruit at the end of summer: “All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs; when shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater!” Fortresses that do not need to be stormed, only shaken, dropping into the mouth of whoever walks up hungry.

Then the muster is inspected, and the inspection is an insult delivered as fact. “Look at your troops”, the prophet says, and the rest of the sentence lands after the text's own break: “they are like your women! The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars.” The gates are not breached; they are open, their bars already burned. So the book mocks the preparations that remain, in a volley of orders nobody can obey in time: “Draw your water for the siege; strengthen your fortresses. Work the clay and tread the mortar; repair the brick kiln!” Store water, tread clay, mend the brickwork. And the answer to all of it is already waiting at the kiln: “There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down and consume you like a young locust. Make yourself many like the young locust; make yourself many like the swarming locust!” Multiply, then. Locusts are what multiplication gets you.

The locust becomes the portrait of the whole empire at the end. “You have multiplied your merchants more than the stars of the sky. The young locust strips the land and flies away.” Merchants beyond counting, and their trade was a locust's trade: strip the land, fly away. The men meant to stay fare no better: “Your guards are like the swarming locust, and your scribes like clouds of locusts that settle on the walls on a cold day. When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where.” Guards and scribes, the sword arm and the record office of the empire, settled on the walls only while it is cold. The sun rises, and no one knows where they went.

At the very end the book finally addresses the man it has never named, by his office alone: “O king of Assyria, your shepherds slumber; your officers sleep. Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them.” Shepherds asleep, and a flock scattered with no gatherer. This series has heard that picture before, prayed in reverse by Micah, who asked the LORD to shepherd His scattered flock home, and promised by Isaiah to people carried back on shoulders. For Assyria there is no such promise. The shepherds sleep, and the scattering is final.

And the book closes on the wound. “There is no healing for your injury; your wound is severe. All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall, for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?” No healing. The word that opened the book's comfort to Judah, that affliction would not rise a second time, finds its mirror here: for Nineveh there is no second rising either, because there is no recovery. The last sound in Nahum is applause, the nations clapping over the grave of the city that fed on them all, and the justification is a question with no defendant left to answer it. Who has not experienced your constant cruelty? The book ends there, and so does this retelling.
